<reflection>
- The addition of initial product and higher catalyst/substrate concentrations in Run 2 successfully broke the degeneracy. Models M8, M6, and M3 have emerged as the clear frontrunners, while product-inhibition models (M12, M17) fell behind, indicating that product effects are likely negligible.
- M8 and M6 both involve a catalyst activation step (reversible vs. irreversible), whereas M3 relies on a dimeric active catalyst (`2cat <=> cat2`). M7 (substrate modification/inhibition) is also still somewhat plausible.
- The aim of differentiating the broad clusters was achieved. Now, the goal is to distinguish between catalyst activation (M6, M8), catalyst dimerization (M3), and substrate-induced effects (M7).
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To strongly differentiate the leading models (M8, M6, M3) and the secondary candidate (M7), we should probe the system at a very low catalyst concentration combined with a maximum substrate concentration. 
By dropping the catalyst concentration to 0.005 (a 10- to 20-fold decrease from previous runs), we will severely penalize M3 if the true mechanism relies on catalyst dimerization, because the concentration of the active dimer scales quadratically with total catalyst ([cat]^2), leading to a disproportionately massive drop in activity compared to the linear dependence in M6 and M8. 
Simultaneously, maximizing the substrate concentration ([S] = 5.0) will push the system deep into the saturation regime. This will strongly test M7, which forms a `catS2` complex, causing its kinetic profile to diverge significantly from models that only form a 1:1 `catS` complex. We will keep initial product at 0.0 to ensure a clean initial rate signal, free from any minor product-related confounding factors, allowing us to isolate the catalyst order and substrate saturation dynamics.
</hypothesis>
